title: Welcome and Table of Contents
summary: What SS2 English Language Second Term is about and a map of every unit.

p: This term you polish your accuracy and widen your range. Grammar: the possessive apostrophe, punctuation marks, sentence types, personal and relative pronouns, reported speech, three-part phrasal verbs and active and passive voice. Oral English: voiced and voiceless consonants, intonation (falling, rising and surprise), rhyme and stress. Writing: formal and informal letters, creative writing and articles. Reading: main points, inference, note-making and critical evaluation. Plus vocabulary from journalism, the environment, building and technology.
At the end of every unit are practice questions. They do not count towards a mark; they help you check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit.

title: Oral English: Voiced and Voiceless Consonants (Revision)
summary: A fuller look at voicing, with minimal pairs, the always-voiced nasals, approximants and the voiceless /h/, and worked examples.

p: A consonant is a speech sound made by partly or completely blocking the air from the lungs. The main way of grouping them is by voicing: voiceless sounds have the vocal cords apart and sound like a puff, hiss or whisper; voiced sounds have the vocal cords together and vibrating. Test by touching your larynx (Adam's apple): 'ssss' (no buzz, voiceless /s/) and 'zzzz' (buzz, voiced /z/).
Study the table.
Nasals (all voiced): /m/ man, /n/ no, /ŋ/ sing; air flows through the nose. Approximants (all voiced): /l/ leg, /r/ run, /w/ wet, /j/ yes; less obstruction. The glottal /h/ (hat) is voiceless.
Odd one out by final sound: push, laugh, breathe, rich. push ends /ʃ/ (voiceless); laugh ends /f/ (voiceless); breathe ends /ð/ (voiced); rich ends /tʃ/ (voiceless). So 'breathe' is the odd one out.
Voiced consonants in 'ledge' /ledʒ/: /l/ and /dʒ/ (the vowel is always voiced but is not a consonant). The final sound of 'judge' is /dʒ/, voiced.

activity: Write the voiceless partner of /b/, /g/, /z/ and /ð/ (/p/, /k/, /s/, /θ/). Are /m/, /n/, /ŋ/ voiced? How can you tell? (Voiced; you feel the buzz.) Transcribe and circle the voiced consonants in: treasure, fishing, village, think, bridges.

check.q: The odd one out for final voicing: push, laugh, breathe, rich

title: Structure: the Possessive Apostrophe
summary: The six rules for showing ownership with an apostrophe, the apostrophe in contractions and the 'its' versus 'it's' rule.

p: The apostrophe shows contraction (do not, don't) and possession (the car of my sister, my sister's car). This lesson is about possession first.
1. Singular nouns not ending in s: add 's: the cat's tail, the woman's car, a student's pen, Mr Bako's house.
2. Plural nouns ending in s: add only an apostrophe: the cats' tails, the students' pens, the Joneses' house.
3. Plural nouns not ending in s: add 's: the children's toys, the men's room, the sheep's field.
4. Singular nouns ending in s: modern British English prefers 's: James's book, the boss's office. (James' book is older and less common; be consistent.)
5. Compound nouns: add 's to the last word: my mother-in-law's car, the Attorney General's office.
6. Joint possession (one thing shared): 's on the last name only: John and Mary's house. Separate possession: 's on both: John's and Mary's houses.
The apostrophe replaces missing letters: it is, it's; you are, you're; they are, they're; who is, who's; do not, don't.

The golden rule: 'it's' is only ever 'it is' or 'it has' ('It's a hot day'). 'Its' with no apostrophe shows possession ('The company is famous for its service'). Similarly 'who's' means 'who is' and 'whose' shows possession.

title: Comprehension: Main Points and Topic Sentences
summary: How to find the main point and the topic sentence of a paragraph by testing candidate sentences, with a worked example on sleep.

sections.h: Main point, details and topic sentence
p: Understanding means getting the author's central message, not just single words. A well-built paragraph has one main point (the controlling idea), often stated in a topic sentence. Supporting details (facts, examples, reasons, statistics, stories) explain or prove it. The topic sentence is often first but may be in the middle or at the end.

1. Read the whole paragraph. 2. Ask: what single idea does the author most want me to understand? 3. Look for a sentence broad enough to cover the others but specific enough to mean something. 4. Test it: do all the other sentences explain, give examples of or develop it?

'A new study has revealed that sleep is far more important than previously thought. While the body rests, the brain is hard at work. It consolidates memories, processing the day's events and storing important information. Furthermore, during sleep the brain clears out toxic by-products that build up while we are awake. This cleaning is vital for long-term brain health. Without enough sleep, a person's ability to learn, focus and make decisions is badly harmed.'

Sentence 1 is a good, general introduction. Sentence 2 makes a clear claim. Sentences 3 to 6 give the evidence (memory, toxin clearing, results of too little sleep). So the best topic sentence is the second: 'While the body rests, the brain is hard at work.'

activity: Find the topic sentence: 'There are several benefits to regular exercise. First, it improves heart health. Second, it helps keep a healthy weight. Finally, it releases endorphins which improve mood and reduce stress.' (The first sentence.) Take three paragraphs from a passage and write each topic sentence.

title: Structure: Question Mark, Exclamation Mark, Colon, Semi-colon and Hyphen
summary: How and when to use five punctuation marks correctly, with examples of common errors.

p: Punctuation tells the reader when to pause, stop or turn. Correct punctuation gives clarity, meaning and rhythm.

sections.h: The question mark and the exclamation mark
p: Question mark (?): at the end of a direct question ('What is your name?'). Do not use it after an indirect question: 'He asked me what my name was.' Exclamation mark (!): ends a sentence or phrase of strong feeling or a forceful command ('What a fantastic goal!' 'Stop!'). Use it sparingly in formal writing.

A colon follows a complete clause and introduces a list, an explanation or a quotation. Correct: 'You will need the following ingredients: flour, eggs, milk and sugar.' Incorrect: 'The ingredients you need are: flour...' (not a complete sentence before the colon). Explanation: 'He had one overriding passion: football.' Quotation: 'The head made an announcement: "All students must return their books by Friday."'

Use 1: join two closely related independent clauses with no conjunction: 'The rain fell relentlessly; the streets began to flood.' Use 2: separate items in a list when the items already contain commas: 'Delegates came from London, England; Paris, France; Tokyo, Japan; and Abuja, Nigeria.'

Join words that act as one adjective before a noun: 'a well-behaved student', 'a last-minute decision' (but 'the student is well behaved'). With prefixes ex-, self-, all-: ex-president, self-confidence. In fractions and numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine: two-thirds, forty-five.

title: Listening: Appreciating Poetry
summary: Tone, purpose and figurative devices in poetry (simile, metaphor, personification, alliteration, onomatopoeia), with a worked analysis of a short poem.

p: Poetry is language at its most musical and concentrated. When you listen to a poem you experience an art, so you attend to the speaker's tone, the poem's purpose and the figures that make its images.

Tone: the speaker's attitude (sad, joyful, angry, nostalgic, sarcastic, reflective). Purpose: why the poem was written: to tell a story (narrative), to describe a scene or feeling (lyric), to mourn (elegy), to praise (ode) or to criticise or mock (satire).

Figures of speech: simile (like or as: 'Her smile was as bright as the sun'); metaphor ('The world is a stage'); personification ('The wind whispered secrets'); alliteration ('The slippery snake slithered silently'); onomatopoeia (words that imitate sounds: buzz, bang, pop, sizzle).

Poem read aloud: 'The city breathes, a beast of steel and stone, / Its heart a steady, pulsing, electric groan. / Cars hiss and growl on wet, black streets, / While lonely people pass in silent beats. / The night is a black velvet cloak, worn and deep, / Under which the tired world falls asleep.'

Tone: sombre, a little threatening, tired. Purpose: to describe the city at night as a living but cold and wearying being. Devices: 'The city breathes' and 'Its heart...groan' are personification; 'hiss and growl' is onomatopoeia; 'lonely people' has alliteration of the l sound; 'The night is a black velvet cloak' is a metaphor.

title: Oral English: Intonation for Surprise and Disbelief
summary: The high-rising tone for surprise and the fall-rise tone for doubt, compared with plain statements and questions.

p: Intonation is the rise and fall of the voice, which adds emotion. Besides normal patterns for statements and questions we can change them to show surprise, shock or disbelief.

The high-rising tone (↗), the 'Really?!' pattern: the voice rises sharply at the end, turning a statement into a question of disbelief. Statement (falling): 'He passed his \exam.' Surprise: 'He passed his ↗exam?!' ('I can't believe it!'). Others: 'You're moving to ↗London?' 'She sold the ↗car?'

The fall-rise tone (V): the voice falls and then rises on the key word. It shows doubt, hesitation or scepticism more than shock: 'He Vpassed his exam' means 'That is what he says, but I am not sure I believe it.'

'The headmaster is \dancing' (neutral statement, informing). 'Is the headmaster /dancing?' (a yes/no question). 'The headmaster is ↗dancing?!' (shocked). The word 'Really?' as a plain question falls ('Rea\lly?'); to express shock it rises high ('↗Really?!').

activity: Write three plain statements and show how you would say each with surprise using ↗. Turn 'The school won the national championship' into a question of disbelief. (The school won the ↗national championship?!) When do you use fall-rise instead of high-rise? (To show doubt rather than shock.)

title: Structure: Sentence Types by Function
summary: The four types of sentence by function (declarative, imperative, interrogative and exclamatory) with their punctuation and examples.

p: Sentences can be sorted by what they do: inform, command, ask or exclaim.

Declarative: makes a statement (fact or opinion); ends with a full stop. 'The sun rises in the east.' 'I enjoy reading historical fiction.' 'He asked me where I lived' is still declarative (a statement about a question).

Imperative: gives a command, request or instruction; the subject 'you' is understood; ends with a full stop or an exclamation mark. 'Close the door.' 'Please take a seat.' 'Stop talking!' 'First, mix the flour and eggs.'
Interrogative: asks a question; ends with a question mark. 'What is the time?' (wh-question) 'Are you feeling better?' (yes/no question) 'You've finished your homework, haven't you?' (tag question).
Exclamatory: expresses strong feeling; ends with an exclamation mark; often begins with 'What' or 'How' but is not a question. 'What a beautiful painting!' 'How incredible that is!'

title: Writing: the Formal Letter of Complaint
summary: The layout, tone and three-paragraph content of a formal letter of complaint, with example wording.

p: A formal letter is professional, respectful and follows a strict format. A letter of complaint expresses dissatisfaction about a product, service or situation and asks for a remedy such as a refund, replacement or apology.

1. Your address at the top right (do not put your name). 2. The date below it. 3. The recipient's address on the left, below the date (for example The Manager, Quality Goods Ltd., 15 Industrial Road, Ikeja, Lagos). 4. Salutation: 'Dear Sir', 'Dear Madam' or 'Dear Sir/Madam'. 5. A heading, underlined and in capitals: 'LETTER OF COMPLAINT: FAULTY HAIR DRYER (MODEL HD-500)'. 6. The body. 7. Closing: 'Yours faithfully' (the only correct ending when you begin 'Dear Sir/Madam'). 8. Your signature. 9. Your full name printed beneath.

Paragraph 1 (purpose): say at once why you are writing, with key details. 'I am writing to complain about a hair dryer I bought from your Ikeja branch on 1st March. The SuperDry HD-500 has proved faulty.'

Paragraph 2 (the problem): describe it factually and precisely, without emotional language. 'The dryer worked for two days, then gave off a burning smell and stopped completely. I have not misused it.'

Paragraph 3 (the remedy): say clearly and reasonably what you want. 'As it is under warranty, I would like it replaced. Otherwise I would accept a full refund of ₦25,000. I attach a copy of the receipt.'
